name: Whale Sanctuary of El Vizcaíno
blurb: Gray whale nurseries, eelgrass lagoons and a desert of pronghorn and coyotes.

tip.title: Thin the eelgrass
tip.text: Eelgrass feeds geese, turtles and seafloor amphipods. Set Eelgrass to -80% and watch the amphipods that gray whales eat, then the whales and killer whales.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Drifting algae that form the base of the open-water food chain. Small plankton-eating fish feed on them.

nodes.name: Eelgrass
nodes.desc: Underwater meadows in sheltered coastal waters. They are grazed by geese and feed small animals when leaves break loose and decay.

nodes.name: Desert shrubs
nodes.desc: Low, sun-loving shrubs of the sandy plains. Browsers eat the foliage, and rodents eat seeds of desert plants like these.

nodes.name: Dagger cactus
nodes.desc: A sprawling columnar cactus of the Baja desert. Pronghorn include cacti in their diet, and succulents are a water source for desert animals.

nodes.name: Seafloor amphipods
nodes.desc: Small crustaceans that live in sediment and on seaweed. Gray whales feed mainly on bottom-dwelling crustaceans like these.

nodes.name: Northern anchovy
nodes.desc: A schooling fish that feeds on plankton. It is food for sea lions and fish-eating birds.

nodes.name: Brant goose
nodes.desc: A small sea goose whose winter diet centres on eelgrass, with sea lettuce and marsh plants as alternatives.

nodes.name: Green sea turtle
nodes.desc: A grazing sea turtle that feeds on seagrass and algae. Marine turtles breed in the reserve lagoons.

nodes.name: Peninsular pronghorn
nodes.desc: The Baja California form of pronghorn, a rare subspecies. Pronghorn eat forbs, shrubs, grasses and cacti.

nodes.name: Black-tailed jackrabbit
nodes.desc: A desert hare that eats shrubs and grasses. It is a common food for coyotes in GloBI records.

nodes.name: Merriam's kangaroo rat
nodes.desc: A seed-eating rodent that rarely drinks, getting water from its food. Snakes, owls and coyotes prey on it.

nodes.name: Gray whale
nodes.desc: Migrates to the reserve lagoons to calve in winter. It scoops up seafloor sediment and strains out crustaceans.

nodes.name: California sea lion
nodes.desc: A coastal seal that breeds and rests on Pacific shores and islands. It feeds mainly on fish and squid.

nodes.name: Osprey
nodes.desc: A fish-eating raptor that hunts along coasts and lagoons. The reserve is home to resident and migratory ospreys.

nodes.name: Glossy snake
nodes.desc: A nocturnal desert snake. GloBI records show it eating kangaroo rats, deer mice and lizards.

nodes.name: Killer whale
nodes.desc: A top marine predator. Orcas are a main predator of gray whale calves and also hunt seals and sea lions.

nodes.name: Coyote
nodes.desc: The top land predator in these records. It eats rodents, hares and pronghorn fawns, and scavenges carcasses.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Strong year-round sun powers desert shrubs and shallow-water meadows alike.

nodes.name: Scarce rain
nodes.desc: This is a very dry region. Many desert animals get water from succulents and their food.

nodes.name: Shallow lagoons
nodes.desc: Warm, sheltered lagoons where eelgrass grows. They are the calving grounds for gray whales each winter.

nodes.name: Cool ocean nutrients
nodes.desc: Cool, nutrient-rich water from the Pacific feeds plankton blooms along the coast. This is general ecology and illustrative.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the sand and the sea.
